The Business Model Canvas shows on one page how HTPL creates, delivers and earns from value. Applied to the asked blocks:
1. Key partners, activities, resources. Partners: Sri Lankan leaf suppliers, recycled-packaging vendors, logistics firms, solar-energy providers, supermarkets/hotels, tea research bodies. 3. questions.solve: An NVA activity costs time and money but adds nothing the customer pays for. Classify each of the six findings, give a fix, and separate them from the ageing process that truly adds value.
questions.answer:
Non-value-added activity: work the customer will not pay for; it adds time and cost but no quality.
1. Labour-heavy transfer of part-aged product between facilities = Moving. Fix: re-layout or co-locate stages, mechanised handling.
2. Barrels left unattended in the staging area while forklift operators do other work = Waiting (idle handling). Fix: dedicated handlers, scheduled material movement, tracking.
3. Bottled spirits waiting in the holding bay for inspectors = Waiting. Fix: more or automated inspection, checks built into the line.
4. Inspecting 10% of all output = Inspecting. Fix: build quality in (TQM, process control, self-checks) and cut the sample.
5. Disorganised warehouse, long dwell of finished goods = Storing. Fix: demand-led production, better layout, faster dispatch (JIT).
6. Haphazard production from unscheduled maintenance = Scheduling. Fix: production planning, preventive maintenance and TPM.
Not NVA: fermentation and 25-year ageing in barrels. This storage creates the flavour customers pay for, so it stays.
Strategic implication: Roshan is right about the craft but not about the waste. Removing the six NVAs cuts cost and lead time, frees working capital, improves margins and delivery, and raises future cash flows, which lifts the value Shrey Industries will pay, while the artisanal core that differentiates the brand stays intact.

(i) AY 2023-24, s.263: Explanation 1(c) to s.263 lets the Commissioner revise any matter not considered and decided in appeal (partial merger). VHIL should price by scenario because the reports disagree on what kind of product this is:
1. Truly unique (two reports: no similar high-end product) = revolutionary product: skimming price to recover R&D and capture early adopters; premium backed by technology and shorter project time.
2. Evolutionary (an improvement buyers must be educated about): price close to value delivered (faster tunnelling, less labour), set after a cost-benefit, competitor and demand study; heavy demos and promotion.

questions.answer:
McKinsey 7S: seven linked elements, three 'hard' (strategy, structure, systems) and four 'soft' (shared values, style, staff, skills). A change in one must be matched by the others. Avigo's crisis came from a lean-cost strategy not supported by its staff, systems and values.
1. Strategy: move from lowest cost at any price to low cost with resilience: crew and aircraft buffers, contingency plans for rule changes like FDTL, the 7% capacity trim until stable.
2. Structure: keep the Crisis Management Group as a standing risk and operations-control unit with clear escalation; link crew planning, network planning, maintenance and compliance.
3. Systems: use the 3% of revenue for AI-based predictive rostering, real-time disruption management, FDTL legality checks and passenger alerts.
4. Shared values: safety, reliability and passenger trust rank equal with cost discipline; early warnings (like FDTL) are acted on, not ignored.
5. Style: participative, transparent leadership; the Board and independent directors oversee operational risk; early reporting of problems is rewarded.
6. Staff: hire the 750+ pilots and staff, keep reserve crew pools, plan the workforce ahead of rule changes, manage fatigue and morale.
7. Skills: train teams in rostering analytics, network recovery, crisis handling and regulatory compliance; build cross-qualified crew.
Alignment: the new strategy works only if the CMG structure, AI systems and enough skilled staff are in place, and values and leadership style back them.
